name: Transconjunctival blepharoplasty / fat repositioning

lead: In this surgery the lower eyelid is opened from the inside, so there is no visible scar, and fat that forms under-eye bags is moved down over the orbital rim to fill the tear trough instead of being removed. The result is a smoother, fresher under-eye with the bag and hollow evened out.

Orbital fat pedicles are released and repositioned into a pocket over the cheek bone area to smooth the lid-cheek transition. Wikipedia notes the inner-lid approach is usually used when there is little excess skin, and additional procedures may be needed if skin laxity is present. Published evidence consists mainly of surgeon case series and retrospective comparisons rather than randomized trials.

paras: It is performed by a qualified surgeon, often with other eyelid or midface procedures. The change is visible once swelling and bruising settle. Candidates are typically those with bags and hollows but little loose skin.

As with eyelid surgery generally, swelling and bruising are common, and eyelid malposition is a reported risk; canthal support techniques may be used to reduce it. It is a surgical procedure performed by qualified surgeons.

angle.text: Candidates choose it to smooth lower-lid bags and fill the tear trough groove without an external scar, so the change is visible once healed. Fat from the bag is moved into the hollow rather than discarded. Evidence comes from surgeon case series rather than randomized trials.

lead: Transconjunctival blepharoplasty is lower-eyelid surgery performed through an incision on the inner surface of the eyelid, leaving no external scar. When combined with fat repositioning, the orbital fat that forms lower-lid bags is moved over the orbital rim to fill the tear trough groove rather than being removed, so the under-eye area looks smoother and less tired from the lid down into the cheek.[1][2][3]

People choose it to reduce under-eye bags and the hollow groove beneath them, which can make a face look older or fatigued, and the repositioning variant is aimed at leaving a smooth lid-cheek transition rather than a hollowed one.[4][5][6] Wikipedia notes the transconjunctival approach is usually used when there is little excess skin, and that additional procedures may be needed if skin laxity is present.[1] Surgical reviews describe a shift over the past three decades from removing lower-lid fat toward preserving and repositioning it, with the transconjunctival route favoured when more than simple skin excision is needed.[7][8]

Published evidence includes surgeon case series, a single-surgeon retrospective comparison of fat planes, and a small number of randomized trials of technique variants and of adding laser resurfacing.[9][10][11][12][13] In looksmaxxing discussion it belongs to the surgical end of the spectrum that commentators call hardmaxxing, applied to the eye area, where tired-looking under-eyes are a common concern.[14][15]
infobox: Inside the lower eyelid (conjunctiva), no external scar[1]
Swelling and bruising over several weeks[1]
Little lid laxity and pseudoherniated fat[5]
Hyaluronic acid filler, fat grafting, transcutaneous approach[6][14]

paras: Wikipedia describes transconjunctival lower blepharoplasty as an inner-lid incision approach that avoids an external scar, in contrast with a transcutaneous incision below the lashes, which allows skin removal.[1] The procedure is typically outpatient and takes one to three hours, with swelling and bruising resolving over several weeks.[1]

A 1995 article described that conventional lower blepharoplasty that removes lower-lid fat can create a hollowed contour deformity, and described arcus marginalis release with fat preservation as an alternative.[4] A 2000 paper described transposing orbital fat pedicles into a subperiosteal pocket over the orbital rim to treat the tear trough.[2]

Wikipedia describes the transcutaneous approach, with an incision just below the lashes, as the one typically used when skin laxity is significant, since it permits skin excision, whereas the transconjunctival approach avoids an external scar.[1] A review states that when a patient has little lid laxity and pseudoherniated periorbital fat, transconjunctival lower blepharoplasty is the treatment of choice, and that it lets the surgeon reposition fat to blend the lid-cheek junction and fill the tear trough.[5] A review of the field lists related techniques as transcutaneous and transconjunctival approaches, fat excision, fat transposition, orbicularis suspension, lateral canthal tightening, malar suspension and skin excision or resurfacing.[16]

Lower-lid bags are produced by the orbital fat pads bulging forward through the septum, and the tear trough is the groove running down and out from the inner corner of the eye where the lid meets the cheek. Wikipedia's article on puffiness notes that ageing brings thinner skin and gradual enlargement of the lower-lid fat pad, and lists many other causes of periorbital swelling such as allergy, sleep loss and fluid retention.[15] A 2007 review describes the tear trough as a groove that casts a shadow that can resemble a dark circle, attributing it to laxity of the orbicularis retaining ligament, herniating orbital fat, midface descent and age-related bone and fat loss.[6]

In the repositioning variant, the surgeon releases the fat pads and advances them as pedicles over the orbital rim into the groove, often securing them with a suture or into a pocket beneath the periosteum or in a plane above it.[2][9] The 2007 review describes several named approaches: Loeb's fat sliding, Hamra's septal reset and Goldberg's transconjunctival repositioning.[6] Reviews note that when too much fat is taken from a lower lid the result can be a hollow, skeletonized look, and a 2017 update says excision is generally reserved for younger patients without midface volume loss, while repositioning suits older patients with midface descent.[7][6]

Wikipedia traces eyelid surgery to the first-century Roman author Celsus, who described an excision to relax the eyelids, and credits Karl Ferdinand von Graefe with coining the word blepharoplasty in 1818.[1] The shift from removing lower-lid fat to preserving and moving it is associated with 1990s and 2000s surgical papers: a 1995 article on arcus marginalis release and orbital fat preservation in midface rejuvenation, and a 2000 description of transposing orbital fat pedicles into a subperiosteal pocket for the tear trough.[4][2]

A 2008 MRI study of orbital changes with age contributed to the anatomical case for repositioning, characterizing contributions to lower eyelid prominence.[17] Later reports include intra-SOOF dissection for lower-lid fat repositioning (2006),[18] fat repositioning with fat grafting for sunken upper eyelids in Asian patients (2011),[19] and a 2024 video article on transconjunctival fat repositioning with barbed sutures.[20]

A 1997 review argued that one operation should not be used for all lower-lid patients, that most patients are best served by combining transconjunctival blepharoplasty with adjunctive procedures, and that the transcutaneous approach has few indications.[21] A 2005 review described traditional fat removal with skin excision as having been replaced by reconstructive blepharoplasty with minimal fat removal, sculpting or repositioning, with chemical peels, microdermabrasion or laser resurfacing as alternatives to skin excision when little skin is redundant.[8] The 2007 tear trough review named fat sliding, septal reset and transconjunctival repositioning as the newer methods and reported excellent results in more than 130 of the authors' own patients, with few complications.[6]

The surgical literature groups the options as transcutaneous versus transconjunctival access, fat excision, fat transposition, orbicularis suspension, lateral canthal tightening, malar suspension and skin excision or resurfacing, chosen according to what is driving the lower-lid appearance.[16] A 2017 review reported that the supraperiosteal and subperiosteal planes give similar cosmetic results and describes a septal reset technique intended to limit unpredictable postoperative fat migration.[7]

Fat grafting and fillers are alternatives or additions. The 2007 review noted that autologous fat pearls and liposculpture carry risks of irregular contours and fat necrosis and often need several sessions, while silicone tear trough implants raised concerns about infection, migration and visibility.[6] Hyaluronic acid fillers are the main minimally invasive option, with effects the same review gave as about three to nine months.[6] The American Society of Plastic Surgeons blog lists fat repositioning, fillers or fat grafts and skin treatments such as PRP as tear trough approaches, with combinations often needed, and calls surgery the only permanent option for the lower lid.[14] A 2024 video article describes using barbed sutures in transconjunctival fat repositioning,[20] and a 2011 report describes orbital fat repositioning with a fat graft for sunken upper eyelids in Asian patients.[19]

Where skin texture or mild laxity is the concern, resurfacing is often paired with the operation instead of skin excision. In a randomized trial transconjunctival blepharoplasty was combined with CO2 laser, and another randomized comparison looked at transconjunctival versus transcutaneous access with the laser.[11][22]

Beyond the 2013 plane comparison described under Clinical studies,[9] Other reports describe intra-SOOF dissection approaches with initial outcomes, and fat repositioning combined with grafting for sunken upper eyelids in Asian patients.[18][19] A review discusses types of tear trough anatomy and treatment options,[3] and an MRI study examined orbital changes with age contributing to lower-lid prominence.[17]
Surgeons' survey data on technique trends exist for members of the American Society of Ophthalmic Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.[23]

A 2020 retrospective series by Cannon and Leatherbarrow covered 150 consecutive patients (mean age 49) of one surgeon operated between April 2010 and October 2019; 141 were very satisfied, five satisfied and four dissatisfied.[12] A 2025 prospective, single-centre cohort of 30 patients (mean age 28, mostly women) used a modified transconjunctival pedicled fat-fascia flap; mean tear-trough grade on a 0 to 4 scale fell from 3.2 to 0.83 at a mean follow-up of 6.2 months, and the authors noted the lack of a control group and short follow-up.[13] The authors also wrote that traditional transconjunctival surgery that only removes septal fat may exacerbate hollowness and that free fat grafting has reported absorption rates of 20 to 90 percent.[13]

The 2013 JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery study was a retrospective single-surgeon review at an ophthalmic plastic surgery practice of 40 patients (mean age 57, mean follow-up 10 months) treated between 2009 and 2011, 20 with fat transposed to the supraperiosteal plane and 20 to the subperiosteal plane. Subperiosteal surgery was described as more meticulous and as causing less bleeding, whereas supraperiosteal surgery was faster but had more bruising, swelling and temporary contour irregularities. Patient satisfaction was 100 percent in both groups, and blinded photo assessment found no significant difference in aesthetic result (P =.45).[9]

A 2025 prospective randomized trial of 40 patients with lower eyelid fat prolapse and tear trough deformity, run from 2020 to 2022, compared a modified transconjunctival technique with traditional transconjunctival blepharoplasty plus orbital fat release. The modified technique had a significantly shorter operating time and maintained outcomes better on tear trough measures and the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale.[10]

A randomized trial in 44 subjects compared transconjunctival blepharoplasty with immediate CO2 laser resurfacing against laser resurfacing two months later. Blepharoplasty alone improved lower-lid bulging in 92 percent of subjects but lower-lid wrinkling worsened in 46 percent; adding laser, immediately or later, significantly improved wrinkles, and no subject developed lid retraction.[11] A further randomized comparison examined the transconjunctival versus transcutaneous approach with the CO2 laser.[22]

Other literature consists of case series and technique reports, including intra-SOOF dissection,[18] fat repositioning with fat graft for Asian upper eyelids,[19] a review of tear trough anatomy types and treatments,[3] and a survey of technique trends among members of the American Society of Ophthalmic Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.[23] A registered trial concerns medial fat pad preservation in upper eyelid blepharoplasty.[24]

Wikipedia describes swelling and bruising that resolve over several weeks, commonly managed with cold compresses and head elevation.[1] In the 2013 comparison, bruising, swelling and temporary contour irregularities were more frequent with the supraperiosteal plane than the subperiosteal plane.[9]

Looksmaxxing coverage divides efforts into softmaxxing (grooming, diet, skincare) and hardmaxxing (cosmetic procedures and surgery).[14][25] Lower-lid surgery is a hardmaxxing option aimed at the eye area, where hollow under-eyes and bags are described as making a face look older or tired.[5][6] Surgeons writing about male patients stress conservative fat handling so that the result keeps a natural eye shape; the ASPS blog notes that what men and women typically want differs and that expectations should be discussed beforehand.[14] The wiki has no loaded forum threads on this procedure.

Wikipedia notes that canthopexy or canthoplasty may be used to reduce eyelid malposition risk, and that swelling and bruising are common and resolve over several weeks, often managed with cold compresses and head elevation.[1] In the 2013 comparison, bleeding, bruising, swelling and temporary contour irregularities were more frequent with the supraperiosteal plane.[9] In the laser trial, no subject developed lower lid retraction.[11] Reviews list lid laxity, festoons and skin texture changes among issues that need recognition before surgery.[16]

A 2017 review groups complications as early (corneal abrasion, orbital hemorrhage, infection), intermediate (lid malposition, strabismus, corneal exposure, epiphora) and late (changes in lid height and contour, hypertrophic scarring, pigmentation), and says lower-lid retraction is among the more frequent problems and visible scarring is most common after the transcutaneous approach.[7] In Cannon and Leatherbarrow's 150-patient series one patient had a bilateral infection requiring abscess drainage and 17 had minor complications, among them temporary inferior oblique palsy (3), residual lateral fat pad prolapse (3), temporary medial ectropion (2), conjunctival granuloma (2) and unilateral lid retraction (1).[12] The ASPS blog notes that surgery on lax lids may cause retraction and that canthopexy or canthoplasty can be added to support the lid.[14] Reviews also stress assessing dry-eye history and eye prominence, which may signal thyroid disease, before surgery.[14]

lore.intro: Public discussion of under-eye surgery is mostly in surgeon and clinic material rather than forum threads, with comparison against fillers and fat grafting as the recurring theme.[6][14]

claims.claim: Moving fat into the tear trough gives a smoother result than removing it
An inside-the-lid incision avoids visible scarring
Fillers can do the same job without surgery
Fat grafting is a lasting alternative to repositioning
The procedure can cause lid problems when done on lax lids
Adding laser resurfacing is needed to treat wrinkling
